theme: Jeroboam II’s prosperity; the northern kingdom’s final decades
readingInstruction: Read 2 Kings 14:1-15:38. These chapters trace the final decades of the northern kingdom, with Jeroboam II’s prosperity and the rapid succession of kings after him. Notice the mixture of God’s mercy and judgment.
settingTheScene: In the first half of the 700s BC, Israel and Judah enjoy a period of prosperity and expansion. Jeroboam II of Israel reigns for forty-one years, and Uzziah (Azariah) in Judah for fifty-two. This is the world of Amos and Hosea, whom you will read next. After Jeroboam II, Israel collapses quickly, with six kings in about thirty years, and the Assyrian empire begins to take its land.
observation: Amaziah of Judah does right “yet not like David his father” and wins a victory over Edom but is defeated by Jehoash of Israel (14:3, 7-14).
Jeroboam II “did what was evil in the sight of the LORD” (14:24).
“He restored the border of Israel from Lebo-hamath as far as the Sea of the Arabah, according to the word of the LORD… which he spoke by his servant Jonah the son of Amittai” (14:25).

“For the LORD saw that the affliction of Israel was very bitter… But the LORD had not said that he would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven, so he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam” (14:26-27).
Azariah (Uzziah) reigns fifty-two years, and “the LORD touched the king, so that he was a leper to the day of his death” (15:5).
Zechariah, Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, and Pekah each reign briefly, with murders and coups (15:8-31).
Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, takes cities and carries people captive (15:19, 29).
Jotham of Judah “did what was right… only the high places were not removed” (15:34-35).
interpretation:
Jeroboam II’s reign is a paradox. By outward measures, it is the best of Israel’s northern kings: territorial expansion, wealth, and stability. But the verdict is the same: “He did what was evil.” The reason for his success is that God saw the bitter affliction of Israel and had compassion. The prosperity is mercy, not approval. This is a striking reminder that material success is not a sign of God’s favor. Israel is flourishing and also rotting. Amos will describe the injustice beneath the prosperity.

Notice the mention of Jonah son of Amittai. The prophet Jonah, whose story you will read in this unit, lived in this time. He delivered a word of hope for Israel’s borders. That same man will be sent to preach to Nineveh, Israel’s future conqueror.

After Jeroboam II’s death, the collapse is quick. The text lists king after king, each murdered by his successor or soon deposed. It is a picture of a nation that has no foundation. Within about thirty years, Assyria will take the land. The speed shows the rottenness of the kingdom.

In Judah, the picture is more stable. Uzziah reigns fifty-two years, and Jotham is faithful. But even the good kings leave the high places. The pattern of partial obedience continues. And Uzziah’s leprosy is mentioned briefly here; 2 Chronicles 26 tells us it came when he proudly entered the temple. Pride undoes even the strong.

The chapters prepare the way for the prophets. The nation’s outward success covers its decay. The rich oppress the poor. Worship goes on while justice is neglected. The coming words of Amos and Hosea will strip off the surface and show what is underneath.
connection: Jesus said, “Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and not do what I tell you?” (Luke 6:46). He warned that wealth can blind us (Mark 10:23-25). The mention of Jonah anticipates Jesus’ sign of Jonah (Matthew 12:39-41). Revelation 3:17 describes a church that says, “I am rich… I need nothing,” and does not know it is wretched. Hebrews 3:13 warns of the deceitfulness of sin.
application:
Ask whether your comfort or success has made you less attentive to God.

Think of a time when God showed mercy that you did not deserve. Thank him.

Pray for the leaders of your nation to seek the LORD in their prosperity.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from mistaking comfort for his approval.
Ask him to strip away surface religion in you.
Thank him for seeing the affliction of Israel and showing mercy.
